We would go with the tree classifier because the score imprved from 0.55 to 0.66. The test_score of 66% represents the fraction that the model labelled correctly which is 66% suggesting some songs were harder to predict. train_score (training accuracy) is 99%; so in each fold the tree is scored on the same 10 inputs it was trained on, means it received a 99% average accuarcy when fitting the data.

title: Spotify Song Attributes
section: Finding the best Tree Depth using a loop
text:
Finding the best Tree Depth using a loop

depths = np.arange(1, 25, 2)
depths

cv_train_scores = []
cv_valid_scores = []

for depth in depths:
    # Create a tree for this depth and evaluate it on ten folds.
    model = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=123, max_depth=depth)
    scores = cross_validate(model, X_train, y_train, cv=10, return_train_score=True)
    cv_train_scores.append(scores["train_score"].mean())
    cv_valid_scores.append(scores["test_score"].mean())

results_df = pd.DataFrame(
    {"mean_train_score": cv_train_scores, "mean_cv_score": cv_valid_scores},
    index=depths,
)
results_df

#Plot
results_df.plot(xlabel= "cv_train_scores", ylabel="cv_valid_scores")
results_df[["mean_train_score", "mean_cv_score"]].plot();

best_max_depth = results_df['mean_cv_score'].idxmax()
best_max_depth

np.int64(5)
















We see from the plot that as depth increases, the training score decreases because we now have a more complex model. At high depth, the tree has memorized training data so its great on training and poor on new predictions (training error is low and validation error is very high)

title: Spotify Song Attributes
section: Fit the final model and score on the test set
text:
Fit the final model and score on the test set

best_model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth = best_max_depth, random_state = 123)
best_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
test_score = best_model.score(X_test, y_test) #note to self: this is the evaluation step taken which is basically getting the score 
test_score

0.745049504950495


We can conclude that we get a 74% accuracy when predicting the preferences of the this listener using a decision tree.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
It genuinely feels like a month has already gone by. The pace here is fast, and it’s so easy to fall behind if you don’t stay on top of labs, worksheets, and readings.
Thankfully I’m not doing this alone, I’ve made some wonderful friends along the way who make things feel a lot more manageable.
My favorite courses so far have been DSCI 521 (Computing Platforms for Data Science) and DSCI 523 (Programming for Data Manipulation). Learning how to build a website, and organize and clean data, all within the first week, has me genuinely excited for what’s ahead. I know I’m in for a ride over the next 10 months. No, seriously, I can’t wait!

title: Languages in Canada
text:
Data: can_lang from the canlang package by Tiffany Timbers (MIT licence). Source: Statistics Canada, Census of Population, 2016. Reproduced and distributed on an “as is” basis with the permission of Statistics Canada.
The goal of this analysis is to explore how Aboriginal languages are used in Canada: how many people speak them at work relative to how many have them as a mother tongue, and which languages are being learned as second languages.

library(tidyverse)

can_lang <- read_csv("can_lang.csv")
head(can_lang)

Next, I found the percentage of people who have Aboriginal languages as their mother tongue and speak it at work. Lastly and just for curiosity, found the aboriginal languages being learned as a second language.

title: About
text:
Background:
I moved to Canada about 6 years ago to study Financial Economics at Carleton University for my Bachelor’s Degree. I worked as a Senior Business Analyst before my Masters in Data Science. Over 3 years at Tangerine Bank, I worked across mobile, web, and platform teams, revamping the client onboarding process for the mobile app, pioneering Tangerine’s new credit card in partnership with Scene+ World Elite Mastercard and later moving to the backend team to help improve the microservices powering products.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science?
This is a loaded question but I’ll sum it up. I got tired of being a BA. I wanted more and I just didn’t know what that was until I worked alongside a data scientist. Watching them build models and experiment with LLMs showed me what that ‘more’ could look like.
